Created 2026-09-22 · HYPE · 922 one-sided taker surges, 2025-03-30 to 2026-06-29 · Source: Exp8 analysis.md, sections 64 and 69 to 71 · All reports

64. What a one-sided taker surge costs the book

A one-sided taker surge widens the HYPE spread, and executions do most of the work.

  • In the 3 minutes around the flow peak the spread reaches 1.8 times its mean over the 12 hours before the surge. 54 to 59 minutes after the run ends it is still 6% wider than that baseline.
  • After a liquidation cascade it is 35% wider in the same bucket and 19% wider 114 to 119 minutes after the run.
  • On 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15, where the book is stored at every order event, executions cause 57% to 63% of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid during a surge, against 32% to 35% in a matched quiet window. Cancellations supply most of the rest.
  • "Push" below means how far one trade moves the surge-side best quote away from the mid.

    It is measured at one book timestamp at which surge-side taker orders clear the whole best level on the side they hit, in bps of the mid. Taker orders that trade in the same microsecond are pooled into one push.

  • The quote does not come back. 50 book updates after a push (counting only updates that move the surge-side best quote or carry a surge-side trade), the quote sits about one more push further from the mid, in every class.
  • Where the quote does return to its level before the push, that takes a median 2,824 ms on a big price move, against 6,032 ms in the control.
Setup: populations, sources and compute

Populations. The 922 one-sided taker surges, tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv, 2025-03-30 to 2026-06-29, classes 561 no big price move, 314 big price move, 47 liquidation cascade. The 915 net-flow boxes, tables/redef2_imb_events_recommended_absgate.csv, appear as a comparison row in Tables 4 and 10. Matched controls are one window per event at the same clock time on the nearest qualifying day, tables/redef2_pop_control_windows.csv.

Per-market-maker rows. tables/redef2_pop_event_mm_F1.csv, 118,269 (event x market maker) rows over 922 events, of which 6,173 carry an accumulation and unwind phase. The comparison file is tables/redef2_pop_event_mm.csv, 126,846 rows over 915 events, controls excluded. These are the files the tilt exhibits were built from. The order-fixed files and the current population of record supersede both; tables/POPULATION_OF_RECORD.md lists the files of record, and the key of Table 4 gives the tilt rerun on the order-fixed files.

Builders. code/f1r0920_reduce_existing.py, code/f1r0921_anchors_and_tilt.py, code/f1r0921_spread_phases.py, code/tick0922_bookevent_build.py with code/tick0922_bookevent.sbatch, code/tick0922_fillgrain_build.py with code/tick0922_fillgrain.sbatch, code/d0921_resign_skew_figures.py, code/f1r0922_tables.py, code/f1r0922_figures.py (the unwind tilt figure with --only tilt_unwind). Compute: two Slurm batch jobs on soal, 256 GB and 16 CPUs each, 4 minutes wall for the book-event build and 34 minutes for the fill-grain build on 2026-09-22; everything else ran inside the interactive allocation. Remaining work and its pre-run contract: plans/plan-2026-09-20-one-sided-surges-placement-skew-and-tick-population.md.

Every exhibit includes 2025-10-10 and 2026-01-31. No date is excluded anywhere on this page.

64.1 Symbols and sign convention

Table 1. Symbols used on this page.

symbol meaning
t0 surge open, the start of the first run minute
t_pv flow-intensity peak, the minute of heaviest surge-side taker flow
t_c pressure peak, the minute at which cumulative in-direction net taker USD counted from t0 stops rising
t1 surge end, the close of the last run minute, so the run is [t0, t1)
t_pp price extreme, the minute of the furthest mid in the surge direction over [t0, t1 + 15 min)
t* one market maker's own inventory peak, the minute of its extreme signed position in the accumulation direction, searched inside [t0, t1)
PRE2H, PRE6H, PRE12H the event's own 2, 6 and 12 hours before t0, used as baselines
SAME the absorption side, whose maker fills built the position
OPP the exit side
a_pre, a_post the best quote on a side immediately before and immediately after every event at one book timestamp
Column key and source

One row is one symbol used somewhere on this page. Every anchor minute is named by its opening time. The surge catalogue tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv stores t0 and the opening time of the last run minute, so t1 is that opening time plus 1 minute, and t1 - t0 reproduces the catalogue's length_min_1m on all 922 events. t_pv, t_c and t_pp come from the same catalogue; t* comes from the F1 population file tables/redef2_pop_event_mm_F1.csv; the baselines and the SAME and OPP labels are set by code/redef2_pop_build.py; a_pre and a_post are read from ts_bookdiff_lt and ts_bookdiff_le.

Every signed quantity on this page is oriented so that the expected direction is positive. A market maker unwinding inventory is expected to bring its exit quote nearer than its absorption quote, so

tilt_bps  = d(SAME) - d(OPP)        positive = the exit quote sits nearer the touch
tilt_size = size(OPP) - size(SAME)  positive = more size rests on the exit side

Both are positive when the market maker is tilted toward getting out.1

64.2 Which minute ends the accumulation phase

The accumulation window ends at t_c, the minute at which the cumulative in-direction net taker dollars counted from t0 stop rising. The median market maker's own inventory peak t* and the price extreme t_pp both land on t_c, a median 3 and 7 minutes after the flow-intensity peak t_pv.

t_c is defined on the flow alone. With d = +1 on a buy surge and -1 on a sell surge, and net(u) the taker buy minus taker sell dollars in minute u,

C(t) = sum over u in [t0, t] of d * net(u)      cumulative in-direction net taker USD
t_c  = argmax of C(t) over the run minutes t in [t0, t1)

The anchors are drawn on two real events, with the flow and the price path beside them, on the one-sided surges page.

Table 2. Minutes from surge open to each anchor.

quantity p5 p25 p50 p75 p95 n

t_c - t0, run open to the pressure peak 2.0 7.0 12.0 20.0 35.0 922
t_c - t_pv, flow peak to pressure peak 0.0 1.0 4.0 9.0 21.0 922
t1 - t0, surge length 4.0 9.0 14.0 23.0 38.0 922
t_pp - t_pv, flow peak to price extreme 0.0 2.0 7.0 15.0 27.0 922
t_pp - t_c, pressure peak to price extreme -7.0 0.0 0.0 9.0 15.0 922

Set-up problem. t* is searched only inside [t0, t1), and t_c is the run's last minute on 76.5% of surges, so "t* lands on t_c" is partly built in: a market maker still accumulating when the run ends has its t* placed in the run's last minute. t* should be searched past t1, as the current section 4.4 rule does out to t1 + 60 min.

Column key and source

Minutes, quantiles across events for the first six rows and across (event x market maker) rows for the last two. t_pp is the furthest mid over [t0, t1 + 15 min); t* is each market maker's own inventory peak. The surge length t1 - t0 is computed from the catalogue and equals its length_min_1m on all 922 events. Source tables/f1r0921_anchor_timing.csv, tables/f1r0921_own_peak_vs_anchor.csv and tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv, built by code/f1r0921_anchors_and_tilt.py and code/f1r0922_tables.py.

  • The pressure peak arrives 4 minutes after the flow peak and almost never before it.

    t_c is at or after t_pv on 99.6% of surges, and the two fall in the same minute on 20.0% (Table 2).

  • The market maker's own inventory peak overlaps t_c.

    The median own peak t* lands on t_c exactly, with 55.9% at or after it, against a median 3 minutes after t_pv with 91.4% at or after it. A window that ends at t_pv closes while most market makers are still accumulating.

  • The price extreme overlaps t_c too.

    t_pp falls in the same minute as t_c at the median, and 7 minutes after t_pv.

Every event-level exhibit on this page therefore ends its accumulation window at t_c, as ACC_c = [t0, t_c) in section 64.4.

64.3 How market makers tilt their quotes

Market makers that accumulated inventory tilt their quotes toward the exit during the unwind.

  • The tilt is +1.55 bps against the market maker's own prior 2 hours.
  • The absorption quote stepping back from the touch supplies most of it.
  • It is read on a 1-minute snapshot of resting orders, not at each order's placement time. Figure 2 gives the placement-time reading.

① Event level. Cuts the market's own clock.

② Market-maker level. Cuts each (event, market maker) row on that market maker's own inventory path.

Table 3. The two families of accumulation and unwind window.

family window rule what it is used for
① event level ACC_c [t0, t_c) the accumulation phase of Figure 3 and Tables 8 and 9 in section 64.4
① event level peak window [t_pv - 1 min, t_pv + 2 min) the flow-peak phase of the same exhibits
① event level post-run buckets 5-minute buckets from t1 - 1 min the phases after the run in the same exhibits
② market-maker level ACC [t0, t*) the folded accumulation reading, Tables 6 and 7, one row per (event, market maker)
② market-maker level UNW [t*, t* + 2 h) Tables 4 and 5, the same rows

Set-up problem: the event-level unwind window UNW_ev = [t_c, t1) is not used. t_c is the run's last minute on 76.5% of surges, so the window is 1 minute long there (7 minutes at p95) and holds almost none of the MMs' unwinding: 42.7% of accumulating MMs peak after t1. Every result built on it has been deleted. The event-level unwind will be the 2 hours from t_c, in buckets of 0-5, 5-10, 10-30, 30-60 and 60-120 minutes. The spread build also writes ACC_pv = [t0, t_pv), which this page does not show.

Column key and source

t* is the market maker's own inventory peak, the minute of its extreme signed position in the accumulation direction, searched inside [t0, t1). That is the rule written into the F1 population file tables/redef2_pop_event_mm_F1.csv by code/redef2_pop_build.py lines 394 to 449, and it is the older section 4.4 rule. The current rule searches the peak out to t1 + 60 minutes, ends the unwind when 60% of the accumulation has been given back, caps it at 6 hours and splits it into minute buckets after t* (project record, section 54). Nothing in this section uses that rule.

Figure 1. Quote tilt toward the exit side during the unwind. Window family ②.

What one mark is, and what the figure excludes

One row per population, over (event x market maker) rows whose market maker accumulated inventory during the event, in the UNW window [t*, t* + 2 h). The dot is the median of that row's unwind tilt minus its own PRE2H tilt; the bar spans p25 to p75. Positive means the exit quote sits nearer the touch than the absorption quote. A side's distance is the market maker's nearest resting order on that side, in bps from the minute's mid, read at each 1-minute grid point and taken as the median over the window's minutes (code/redef2_pop_orders.py), so it records where orders sat during the minute. The net-flow row is negated from its published sign (project record, section 50). The accumulation rows are folded below Table 5.

Figure 2. Distance to the touch at order placement, by window. Window family ②, on the current section 4.4 rule.

What one mark is, and what the figure excludes

Population. The 922 one-sided surges. Rows are (event x market maker) pairs in the population of record, the D3d active market makers (data/f1d3d_pairs.parquet), cut to the accumulators of the OR rule, the population of record for these phases. Every row of data/f1u0922_phase_rows.parquet is such an accumulator. The phase rule is the current section 4.4 rule, own_peak_60_t60: t* is the market maker's own inventory peak searched out to t1 + 60 min, and T60 is the minutes from t* until 60% of the accumulation is given back, capped at 360. This t* differs from the one of Figure 1, which is searched inside [t0, t1).

Measure. Each limit order (ALO or GTC) is read once, at its own placement time t, against the book row of ts_bookdiff_lt strictly before t. Its distance is d = 1e4 * (bid_0 - price) / mid for a bid and 1e4 * (price - ask_0) / mid for an ask, in bps of the mid strictly before t, so 0 is at the same-side best quote and positive is behind it. An order enters a window when its placement time falls inside it; no 1-minute grid is used. A row's side distance is the size-weighted mean of d over that side's orders placed in the window. Panel B subtracts the same row's PRE2H value. Panel C is d(SAME) - d(OPP) on rows with orders on both sides.

Weighting. One event, one vote: each event's value is the median across its accumulating market makers' rows. The dot is the median across events and the bar spans p25 to p75 across events. Every window holds all 922 events. Rows with a tilt: PRE2H 30,064, PRE30 28,453, ACC 29,243, 0-5 min 25,183, 5-10 min 25,161, 10-30 min 27,336, UNW 29,701.

Windows. PRE2H [t0 - 2 h, t0), PRE30 [t0 - 30 min, t0), ACC [t0, t*), the buckets [t*, t* + 5), [t* + 5, t* + 10) and [t* + 10, t* + 30) minutes, UNW [t*, t* + T60). The windows overlap: PRE30 sits inside PRE2H, and the three buckets start at t* like UNW, so an order can count in more than one window, and UNW is not the average of the buckets. The grey band separates the pre-event windows from the market maker's own phases. PRE12H is not drawn because the order panel starts 2 hours before t0.

Source. tables/place0922_quantiles.csv (PRE2H, PRE30, ACC, UNW levels), tables/place0922_paired_change.csv (PRE30, ACC, UNW changes) and tables/place0922_buckets.csv (the three buckets, basis level and change), rows population = F1d3d, cut = accumulators (OR rule), weighting = one event one vote, measures d_place_SAME_bps, d_place_OPP_bps and tilt_place_bps. Built by code/place0922_build.py and code/place0922_reduce.py, drawn by code/place0922d_figure.py.

  • Before the surge the two sides are placed at the same distance.

    The placement tilt is +0.03 bps in PRE2H and +0.07 bps in PRE30, with the absorption side at 11.30 bps and the exit side at 11.93 bps behind the touch in PRE2H.

  • At placement the accumulation phase already leans toward the exit.

    In ACC the tilt is +0.63 bps against the market maker's own PRE2H, positive on 70.5% of events. The absorption quote is placed 0.79 bps further back and the exit quote 0.18 bps further back. The minute snapshot of the folded Table 6 reads the same phase at -13.10 bps; pooled over rows like that table, the placement reading is +0.54 bps.

  • The tilt is largest in the first 5 minutes after the own peak and fades by 30 minutes.

    It is +1.13 bps in [t*, t* + 5), +0.84 bps in the next 5 minutes and +0.49 bps in [t* + 10, t* + 30). The absorption side supplies it: 0-5 minutes after t* that quote is placed 0.74 bps further back than in PRE2H and the exit quote 0.11 bps nearer. Over the whole unwind the change is +1.44 bps, positive on 88.7% of events; pooled over rows it is +1.52 bps, against +1.55 bps on the snapshot of Figure 1.

A tilt is a difference of two distances, so its size alone does not say which side moved.

64.4 Spread, depth and taker cost by phase

In the 3 minutes around the flow peak the spread reaches 1.8 times its mean over the 12 hours before the surge, and after a liquidation cascade it is still 35% wider than that baseline 54 to 59 minutes after the run ends.

The spread statistic.

  • The quoted spread is the best ask minus the best bid in ts_bookdiff_lt, in cents. HYPE's tick is $0.001, or 0.1 cents.
  • For the median event the median quoted spread is one tick in every phase, from 12 hours before t0 to about 2 hours after t1.
  • The mean moves with the surge, from 0.25 cents over PRE2H to 0.44 cents in the peak window, the 3 minutes [t_pv - 1 min, t_pv + 2 min) around the flow peak, because it counts the moments when the spread opens beyond one tick.
  • This section reports the mean, taken over the book rows in each minute and then over the minutes of a phase.

The surge-side effective half-spread. Over the surge-side taker orders i in a phase,

EHS = [ sum over i of v_i * 1e4 * s * (p_i - m_i) / m_i ]  /  [ sum over i of v_i ]
  • v_i is the order's USD notional, p_i its volume-weighted fill price, m_i the ts_bookdiff_lt mid at the order's own microsecond, and s = +1 on a buy surge and -1 on a sell surge, so a positive value is a cost to the taker.
  • It prices every fill of the order against the mid before the trade, and most surge-side dollars fill beyond the best quote: 77% over PRE2H and 94% in the peak window, in a sample of 20 surges.
  • For the median event it is 3.91 bps against 0.36 bps for half the quoted spread over PRE2H, and 9.69 against 0.63 in the peak window.
How the spread and the effective half-spread are computed
  • Book rows. Each row of ts_bookdiff_lt is the book strictly before every event at one timestamp. A row counts when it has both a best bid and a best ask and the bid is below the ask. From 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15 the table has one row per book update, about 610 rows a minute, and 398 of the 917 surges fall in this range. On every other date it has one row per fill timestamp, about 75 to 180 rows a minute, so each row is the book just before a fill; 519 surges fall there. Every surge's windows, from PRE12H to about 2 hours after t1, sit on one side of both dates, so each event's ratio and difference uses one grain; the cents levels in the top panel of Figure 3 pool both grains.
  • Grain. The peak-window ratio of 1.82 pools the two grains: it is 1.96 on the fill-grain dates and 1.65 on the book-event dates, and from t1 - 1 min onward the two agree to within 0.06.
  • Minute value. The plain mean of ask_0 - bid_0 over the minute's rows. The mean is taken over book rows, each row weighted equally, however long its book lasted. On the book-event dates it is within 2% of a mean weighted by how long each book lasted, over PRE2H and in the peak window, in a sample of 12 surges. Minutes with no row are dropped.
  • Phase value. The plain mean of the minute values over the phase, each minute counted once. The buckets after the run are 5 minutes each, counted from t1 - 1 min, the opening of the run's last minute.
  • Baseline and events. Tables 8 and 9 and the middle panel of Figure 3 divide each event's phase value by the same statistic over that event's PRE12H, the mean of its 720 minute values. Every panel plots the median across events, and the top panel shades p25 to p75.
  • The two one-tick statistics. The median statistic takes each minute's median book row, then the median over the phase's minutes, then the median across events; it is one tick in every phase, and in the peak window about half the events have their own median above one tick. The share statistic counts a phase's minutes whose mean spread is at most 1.5 ticks; its median across events is 16.5% over PRE12H, 10.0% over PRE2H and 0% from t0 to about 2 hours after t1. The two agree because most book rows in a minute sit at one tick while a few wide ones lift the minute's mean above 1.5 ticks. tables/f1r0921_spread_phase_levels.csv holds the mean in cents, ticks and bps, the share of minutes at one tick and the p90 over minutes; p75 and p95 per event are in tables/f1r0921_spread_phase_event.csv.
  • Effective half-spread inputs. Orders from grouped_trade_oid with crossed = True, one row per taker order at one microsecond. Auto-deleveraging fills are excluded and liquidation orders are included, and every wallet on the surge side counts. The mid m_i matches at the order's exact microsecond for at least 99.9% of taker USD on every date, on both grains. The bottom panel of Figure 3 and the findings below subtract the same event's PRE2H value, computed the same way.
  • Code. The per-minute panel data/review0917_mktq_1m/ is built by code/review0917_mktquality_build.py; the phases, ratios and levels by code/f1r0921_spread_phases.py into tables/f1r0921_spread_phase_{levels,ratios,event}.csv. code/spread0922_check.py reproduces every number in this block.

    It reaches 1.82 times the event's own 12-hour mean in the peak window and is down to 1.46 in the bucket [t1 - 1, t1 + 4) min (Table 8).

    Surge-side resting size within 10 bps of the mid stays at 1.01 to 1.09 times its own PRE2H level at every phase, including the peak window, with p25 between 0.76 and 0.84 across events and p75 between 1.31 and 1.53. The surge is absorbed by a wider quoted spread while near depth holds.

    The effective half-spread is 5.26 bps above the event's own prior 2 hours in the peak window, 15.10 bps for cascades, and 0.42 bps in the bucket [t1 - 1, t1 + 4) min. From t1 + 4 min onward it runs 1.0 to 1.8 bps below that baseline.

The last point sits opposite the net-flow result of section 4.10 on the main page (project record, section 57), which found surge-side takers paying 0.61 bps more in the first 10 minutes after the event and 0.28 bps more 20 to 30 minutes after it. The baselines differ: that result uses a matched control window on another day, this page the event's own preceding 2 hours, which are themselves already wide. A market that is quiet by its own recent standard can still be expensive by the standard of an ordinary day.

64.5 What moves the surge-side quote

On 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15, where the book is stored at every book update, executions cause 57% to 63% of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid during a surge, against 32% to 35% in a matched quiet window, a ratio of 1.7 to 1.9. The 93.5% single-episode reading (project record, sections 28 and 30) uses the same grain and the same side. It is a property of the most intense interval of one December 2025 episode.

Set-up problem. On a one-sided surge the book-event and fill-grain builds end the surge window at t1 - 1 min, so every book-update number in sections 64.5 to 64.7, 69 and 70 leaves out the run's last minute, while the net-flow boxes and the controls use the full [t0, t1). The surge window should be [t0, t1).

Setup: the measure, the side, and why the grain matters

A book update is one distinct timestamp at which the exchange recorded at least one HYPE order being placed, cancelled, triggered or filled. Everything recorded at that timestamp belongs to the same book update: a taker's order, the fills it produced, and other traders' new quotes and cancels. The book is read twice per book update, strictly before anything at that timestamp (ts_bookdiff_lt) and after the fills and then the cancels (ts_bookdiff_le). A book update where the surge-side best price stays where it was has c = 0. It adds nothing to the travel in either direction, so it drops out of every travel share. These updates are a median 81% of a surge window's book updates (Table 11).

What one book update holds, measured on 2025-12-17
  • The book updates are exactly the order and fill timestamps. On 2025-12-17 the 895,128 ts_bookdiff_lt keys equal the union of every placement time and status time of a non-rejected order in the order feed and every fill time, with none missing on either side. A rejected order, such as a post-only order that would have crossed the book, never rests and adds no book update of its own. The date's file also carries 5,360 later timestamps, the cancel and fill times of orders placed that day and closed on a later day; the counts below use the 889,768 book updates stamped on the date.
  • Many events share one book update. A book update holds a median of 12 events (p5 1, p25 5, p75 26, p95 64), counting each order placed, each order cancelled and each trade once, and 93.5% of book updates hold two or more. Consecutive book updates are a median 87 ms apart (p5 50 ms, p95 193 ms).
  • Most book updates are quote updates. 13.1% of book updates carry a fill. 72.6% carry both new orders and cancels, 8.6% only new orders and 5.6% only cancels, all without a fill.
  • Inside a surge more book updates carry a fill. In the buy surge of Figure 5, 02:56 to 03:06 UTC, 35.6% of the 6,530 book updates carry a fill and a book update holds a median of 26 events.

Source tables/tickcls0922_rowdef.csv, built by code/tickcls0922_rowdef.py.

The side measured is the one the takers consumed, the ask on a buy surge and the bid on a sell surge. With m the ts_bookdiff_lt mid and the sign chosen so that away from the mid is positive:

c_bps = 1e4 * s * (a_post - a_pre) / m      what the events at this timestamp did
r_bps = 1e4 * s * (a_next - a_post) / m     what happened before the next book update

A book update with c > 0 is classified trade when a surge-side taker at that timestamp covered the whole a_pre level (or reached two or more levels), mixed when a taker was present but did not cover it, and cancel when no taker was present. A book update with c < 0 is a post, a quote arriving inside the previous best, and one with c = 0 is no change.

The replacement depth is the size standing at the surge-side best k kept updates after the pushing execution, over the size that stood on the level the execution ate:

D(k) = q(best, just after the k-th kept update after the push) / q(a_pre)

k counts kept updates only. The build keeps a book update when the surge-side best price moved or a surge-side taker traded at it, a median 25% of a surge window's book updates, and drops the rest before any horizon is counted. D(k) reads the best-level size at the book update right after the k-th kept update following the push, and the event-time horizons of section 64.7 count the same kept updates. D(k) > 1 means the level now standing is thicker than the one that was eaten. It is a different object from the phi of section 69, which is read at the next fill and not at a fixed count of updates.

r_bps is zero by construction at this grain, because lt(t_i+1) is the same book state as le(t_i) when consecutive rows are consecutive book updates. Measured, it is non-zero on 0.03% to 0.11% of kept updates and is kept only as a validation column. Replenishment here is the next post update, not a gap between two updates. The a_post to a_next gap carries information only when the grain is coarser than the book updates, which is the fill grain of sections 64.6 and 69.

Scope. 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15 only, the range where the phase tables carry a row at every book update. That is 398 of the 922 surges, 397 of the 915 boxes and 243 controls, with 33.4 million kept updates in the build's part files; a median surge window holds 8,572 book updates in all. The surge window is the build's [t0, t1 - 1 min) on a one-sided surge, one minute shorter than the run, and [t0, t1) on a net-flow box or a control. Outside the range the tables are keyed at fill microseconds, so "the next row" means something else and the two cannot be pooled; section 64.6 measures every date at fill grain instead.

  • A surge nearly doubles the execution share against a matched quiet window.

  • The three classes sit within 6 points of each other.

  • The push per execution rises with the size of the print, and the top decile is where it becomes large.

    On the one-sided surges with a big price move, the median push runs 1.26 bps at decile 1 and 2.35 at decile 8, then 3.24 at decile 9 and 7.11 at decile 10. Median surge-side size at decile 10 is 2,985 HYPE against 367 at decile 8.

  • The level that replaces the one eaten is always thicker, and least so in the middle deciles.

    On the big-price-move class the ratio is 4.58 at decile 1, sits in a basin of 1.70 to 1.83 over deciles 4 to 8, and rises to 3.21 at decile 10. Small prints eat a thin touch and expose a thick level behind it; large prints walk several levels and stop at a thick one.

  • During a surge the replacement level is thinner than in a quiet window.

    On the big-price-move class D(1) is 1.94 on the one-sided surges against 2.73 in the control, and D(50) is 2.52 against 4.14 (Table 12). Every class reads the same way.

Executions move the surge-side quote on 3.0% of a surge's book updates and carry 59.7% of its travel away from the mid. Cancels move it on 4.9% of book updates and carry 37.1%. In the matched control the same two classes carry 34.6% and 62.1%.

  • book updates: the class's book updates over every book update in the window. no change is every book update with c = 0; "of which a taker traded" is the part of it where a surge-side taker traded and the best price stayed put.
  • travel away: the sum of c over the class's book updates with c > 0, over the same sum across all book updates. Only trade, mixed and cancel have c > 0.
  • travel back: the sum of -c over book updates with c < 0. A post is defined as a book update with c < 0, so it carries all of this travel.
  • surge, box, control: one-sided surges, net-flow boxes and matched controls.

By price class the trade share of travel away is 57.2% (no big price move), 63.0% (big price move) and 61.7% (liquidation cascade) on the surges, and 34.3%, 35.0% and 31.8% on the controls, the values of Table 10. The book-update shares differ across price classes by at most 4 points. Pooled over all book updates instead of taking the median across units, the trade share of travel away is 69.2% on the surges, 61.5% on the boxes and 37.2% on the controls, because the longest and busiest surges hold the most book updates. A median surge window holds 8,572 book updates, a box 18,804 and a control 18,515. The full p5, p25, p50, p75 and p95 set for every cell, pooled and by price class, is in tables/tickcls0922_classes_long.csv; one row per unit is in tables/tickcls0922_unit_counts.csv. Built by code/tickcls0922_table.py, which checks every unit's shares against tables/tick0922b_event_decomp.csv and every class median against tables/tick0922b_headline.csv.

  • A trade update pushes the quote further than a cancel update.

    Within a surge the mean push of a trade update is a median 2.88 bps of the mid, against 1.22 bps for a cancel update; the trade push is the larger of the two in every one of the 393 surges. A print that clears a level exposes the gap behind it.

  • Posts are the most common update that moves the quote, and they carry all of its travel back toward the mid.

    They are 10.8% of a surge's book updates and 6.7% of a control's. Over the window the travel back is a median 90% of the travel away on the surges and 101% on the controls.

  • Most book updates leave the surge-side best price where it was.

    80.8% of a surge's book updates have c = 0. On 5.0% of all book updates a surge-side taker traded and the best price stayed put; section 69 measures what such prints consume.

  • mixed updates are rare in every population.

    They are 0.2% to 0.4% of book updates and carry 3.1% of the travel away. The mixed example of Figure 5 is a cancel the exchange processed ahead of the taker's order.

Figure 5. One book update of each class in a December 2025 buy surge.

What one panel shows, and what each example means

Each row is one book update from the one-sided buy surge of 2025-12-17, 02:56 to 03:06 UTC, a big-price-move event, so the surge side is the ask. The left half of a panel is the ask ladder strictly before the update (lt), the right half the ladder after its fills and then its cancels (le), five levels each. Bar length is the resting size in HYPE and the vertical axis is the price. The arrow in the center runs from a_pre to a_post. The text beside each panel gives c in bps of the lt mid, in dollars and in price ticks of $0.001, the taker's fills at that timestamp from the fill feed, and the cancels and new orders from the order feed. A level that appears only on the right was already resting behind the fifth level. In the mixed panel the eaten level is split into the 1.24 HYPE bought (green) and the 74.74 HYPE cancelled (grey); the green segment is drawn wider than 1.24 HYPE so that it shows.

  • Trade, 02:56:49.095. One market buy of 79.55 HYPE takes all 75.00 HYPE at $26.382 and 4.55 of the 148.29 at $26.384. The best ask moves up 2 price ticks, +0.76 bps. The rest of the ladder is the same before and after.
  • Mixed, 03:01:11.638. An IOC buy limited at $26.879 for up to 310.08 HYPE receives 1.24 HYPE, the remainder of one resting order. A second order of 74.74 HYPE at $26.879, from the same wallet, is cancelled at the same timestamp, and the best ask moves up 1 price tick, +0.37 bps. The buyer would have filled against the 74.74 HYPE had it still been resting, so the exchange processed the cancel first. The lt and le books record only that both happened at this timestamp.
  • Cancel, 02:56:50.898. The 68.75 HYPE resting at $26.382 is cancelled and the update carries no surge-side taker. The best ask moves up 2 price ticks, +0.76 bps.
  • Post, 02:56:49.493. A new order of 68.75 HYPE arrives at $26.382, inside the previous best of $26.384, and the best ask moves down 2 price ticks, -0.76 bps.

Source tables/tickcls0922_examples.csv, one row per level drawn. Built by code/tickcls0922_figure.py, which checks each example's c and class against the part file of code/tick0922_bookevent_build.py.

The trade, post and cancel examples are three consecutive moves of the best ask. The wallet whose 75.00 HYPE was bought at $26.382 posted 68.75 HYPE at the same price 0.4 seconds later and cancelled it 1.4 seconds after that. In 1.8 seconds the quote traveled 1.52 bps away from the mid, half through the trade and half through the cancel, and 0.76 bps back through the post. Part of the cancel travel at this grain is this round trip: a quote posted inside the best and withdrawn about a second later. Counted between fills (section 64.6) it nets out.

64.6 The same measure between fills, on every date

Compared at consecutive fill timestamps instead of at every order event, executions cause a median 76.2% of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid during a surge and 58.7% in a matched quiet window, over every date (Table 14).

  • The gap holds in each calendar period: 83.8% against 70.5% over 2025-03-30 to 2025-09-26, 71.1% against 52.2% over 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15, and 71.8% against 56.3% over 2026-04-16 to 2026-06-30. Medians across events, each event in the period where it starts (Table 15).
  • The surge effect of section 64.5 therefore holds on the 57% of events the book-event comparison cannot reach.
  • The level depends on the grain: on the same events, comparing at fills raises the execution share by 12 points on the surges and 17 on the controls.
Setup: the fill grain, and how it relates to the book-event grain

Outside 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15 the phase tables hold a row only where a fill occurred. On all 244 such dates used here, every key is a taker or maker fill timestamp and no fill timestamp is missing from the table. At fill grain a row is one fill timestamp:

c_bps = 1e4 * s * (le(t_i)   - lt(t_i)) / m     the fills and cancels at fill timestamp t_i
r_bps = 1e4 * s * (lt(t_i+1) - le(t_i)) / m     every placement and cancel before the next fill

Gross travel away from the mid is the positive part of c plus the positive part of r. The execution share is the travel from trade fill timestamps over that total, and the between-fill share is the positive part of r over the same total. A fill timestamp is trade when the executed surge-side size at it covers the whole lt level or the taker reached two levels. Executed size is the larger of the taker size consuming that side and the maker size resting on it, because the maker and taker row sets do not balance on 2025-03-24 to 2025-05-25.

Inside the range the same code subsets the book updates to the fill timestamps, which gives the same object, and computes the book-event grain beside it with the same classification. At book-event grain it reproduces tables/tick0922b_event_decomp.csv on all 3,109 (event x side x phase) units, with a largest difference of 1.1e-16.

Why the grain moves the level. A cancel that pulls the best quote away and a placement that restores it before the next fill both count as travel at book-event grain, and they net to zero between two fills. Counting between fills removes that round trip. Gross travel falls to 0.83 of its book-event value on the surges and to 0.67 on the controls, whose quotes flicker more, so the control's execution share rises more.

Scope. 910 of the 922 surges, all 915 boxes and all 558 control windows, 75.3 million kept rows over both grains. The 12 surges without a unit are one-minute runs, t1 = t0 + 1 min, so the build's surge window [t0, t1 - 1 min) is empty on them. Compute: one Slurm batch job on soal, 256 GB and 16 CPUs, 2026-09-22, 34 minutes wall, 17.5 GiB peak memory, code/tick0922_fillgrain_build.py with code/tick0922_fillgrain.sbatch.

  • At fill grain the surge raises the execution share above its control in every period.

    Surges sit 13.3, 18.9 and 15.4 points above the matched controls in the three periods and the net-flow boxes 9.4, 14.9 and 11.0 points (Table 15). Across every date the medians are 0.762 on the surges and 0.587 on the controls (Table 14).

  • Counting between fills raises the level on every unit.

    On the same in-range units the fill-grain share is higher on 100% of them, by a median 11.9 points on the surges, 14.2 on the boxes and 16.9 on the controls (Table 13). The surge-over-control gap on those events narrows from 24.9 points at book-event grain to 18.9 at fill grain.

  • The two grains measure different things, so each keeps its own role.

    The book-event share is the measure of record for the 43% of events it covers. The fill-grain share is the one available on every date, and its surge-over-control gap carries the claim to the other 57%.

  • The result survives dropping the incomplete early fill dates.

    Dropping the events that start on 2025-03-24 to 2025-05-25 moves the surge median from 0.762 to 0.752 and the control median from 0.587 to 0.571.

Remark that needs attention. Before 2025-09-27 the fill-grain execution share is 13 to 18 points higher than inside the range, on surges, boxes and controls alike: 0.838, 0.799 and 0.705 against 0.711, 0.671 and 0.522, with less travel between fills, 0.109 against 0.197 on the surges.

  • The storage format is ruled out. 2026-04-16 to 2026-06-30 is stored the same way as the early months and matches the in-range values.
  • The incomplete early fill record is ruled out too. The later part of the early period, 2025-05-26 to 2025-09-26, reads higher still, 0.846 on the surges against 0.819 on the incomplete dates.
  • Candidate cause: fewer quote placements and cancels per fill in the early months.
  • Test: count order placements and cancels per fill by month from the order store, and check that the monthly count tracks the between-fill share.

64.7 How fast the quote comes back

Every number in this section is the share of one execution's push that is no longer standing at a horizon,

R(h) = 1 - (level at h - level before the push) / push

so R = 0 leaves the push intact, R = 1 returns the quote to its pre-execution level and R < 0 means the quote traveled further out. Horizons h are counted in kept updates first, the book updates at which the surge-side best price moved or a surge-side taker traded, and in clock time second.

The push stands in event time and in clock time alike.

  • 50 kept updates after an execution moved the surge-side quote, the quote sits 0.83 to 1.18 further pushes away from the mid, depending on the class.
  • 30 seconds after the execution it sits 0.94 to 1.74 further pushes out.
  • The matched controls barely move. Across their three classes the share reverted sits within 0.02 of zero at every horizon, except 100 milliseconds, where it runs 0.02 to 0.11, and 20 kept updates and 30 seconds on the 32-event cascade class, where the quote drifts 0.13 and 0.12 further out.

Figure 6. Share of the push reverted, by horizon.

What one mark is, and what the figure excludes

Every kept update inside the surge window where an execution pushed the surge-side best quote away from the mid. The vertical axis is the share of that push reverted by the horizon: zero means the quote has not moved back, one means it is back at its pre-execution level, and a negative value means it has traveled further out. Top panel counts horizons in kept updates, the axis's "book events", bottom panel in clock time; both axes are ordered categories drawn at equal spacing, not to scale. Each line is the median within an event, then the median across events. The control line is its no-big-move class. The big-price-move control sits within 0.03 of it at every horizon; the 32-event cascade control sits within 0.02 except at 100 milliseconds, 20 kept updates and 30 seconds, where it is 0.07, 0.13 and 0.12 away.

  • The push survives the next kept update.

    At one kept update the share reverted is 0.000 to 0.069 in every class (Table 16).

  • 50 kept updates later the quote has traveled further out in every class.

    It sits 1.18 pushes further out on a big price move, 0.94 in a liquidation cascade and 0.83 with no big move, against 0.00 in each class's own matched control.

  • The same holds at 30 seconds, so the event clock and the wall clock agree.

    The quote sits 1.74, 1.32 and 0.94 further pushes out on the three surge classes, against 0.00, 0.12 and 0.00 in their own matched controls.

  • The quote crosses its old level sooner during a surge while drifting further from it.

    A push returns to its pre-execution level in a median 2,824 ms on a big-price-move surge against 6,032 ms in its matched control, while book updates arrive a median 88 ms apart inside a surge window against 90 ms in a control, so the arrival rate is not what makes the surge look quicker. Gross travel away from the mid is 2,094 bps in a surge window against 1,545 bps in the control (Table 19), so the surge-side quote crosses its old level more often on the way to sitting further out.

  • Over the whole window the surge-side quote ends further from the mid than it started.

    Gross travel toward the mid is 0.89 to 0.91 times gross travel away from it on the surges and 1.01 in every control class, and the net move is +97 to +191 bps away from the mid on the surges against -8 to -26 bps in the controls (Table 19).

  • At fill grain, on every date, the push stands in clock time too.

    On big-price-move surges a median 5% of a push has reverted after 1 second inside the book-event range and 16% outside it, none of it is back at 5 seconds, and by 30 seconds the quote has traveled a further 1.71 to 1.73 pushes out (Table 18).

Column key and source

One row is a population and class over the surge window at book-event grain. travel away is the gross travel of the surge-side best quote away from the mid, summed over the window's book updates; back over away divides the gross travel toward the mid by it, so a value below 1 leaves the quote further out than it started; net move is the signed end-to-start change, positive away from the mid. All three are p5 to p95 across (event x side) units, one value per line. ms to the next book update is the median within a unit, over its kept updates, of the time to the next book update of any kind, then the median across units; it is the arrival rate that makes the event clock and the wall clock differ. n counts units. Source tables/tick0922b_headline.csv and tables/tick0922b_event_decomp.csv.

Section 69 reads the same object at the next trade in place of a fixed horizon.

64.8 Where this sits in the order-book resiliency literature

Lining up on aggressive orders and tracking the spread, the best quote and the depth over the following book updates is the design of Biais, Hillion and Spatt (1995) and of Degryse, de Jong, van Ravenswaaij and Wuyts (2005). Large (2007) is the hazard-model version, which estimates a replenishment intensity in place of a level path and is the natural next step once the question becomes how long resilience takes.

Design choices taken from that literature:

  • Horizons are counted in book updates first and clock time second, because the arrival rate itself changes during a surge.
  • Prints are ranked into deciles within their own event, so the comparison is between prints of the same episode.
  • Every number carries a matched quiet-window benchmark, because the level alone has no meaning.

64.9 The book tables

ts_bookdiff_lt is a reconstruction of the book strictly before every event at a timestamp.

  • Its best quotes match the last raw Tardis snapshot on 55% to 85% of rows.
  • Its row grain changes by date.
What was verified, and on which days

Three phase tables exist for HYPE. ts_bookdiff_lt is the book strictly before every event at a timestamp. ts_bookdiff without a suffix is after arrivals and updates but before fills, so it is not a post-trade book. ts_bookdiff_le is after fills and then cancellations, and it is the post-trade state. On 2025-12-17, at taker-fill microseconds, lt and the middle phase agree on 87.2% of best prices while the middle phase and le differ on 65% of best-ask sizes.

The row grain changes by date. On 2025-09-27 to 2026-04-15 all three are keyed at every book update: 895,128 rows on 2025-12-17 against 116,988 taker-fill microseconds, and 100% of the extra timestamps are order placement or status timestamps. Outside that range they are keyed at fill microseconds only; on all 244 out-of-range dates used in section 64.6, every key is a taker or maker fill timestamp. Storage differs too, (timestamp, state_id) joined to ts_bookdiff_states inside the range and 20 inline price and amount columns outside it.

ts_bookdiff_lt was never overwritten by the forder work. The 2026-07-30 ordered walker replaced only p_mid in grouped_trade_oid and grouped_trade_oid_leverage on 201 dates; restore_legacy_pmid.py reverted it and archived the bad values as pmid_ordered_invalid_2025-09-27_2026-04-15/. Recomputing p_mid from today's lt reproduces the stored value on 100.0000% of taker rows on 2025-12-17, inside the overwrite window, and on 99.98% on 2025-04-15, and p_mid = p_0 + s * hs_component / size holds on 100% of rows on all three days tested. The forder ceiling defect is a different table: kcalc3.py's gord = tag * 10^7 + forder overflow in k_fills_by_day on 46 dates.

64.10 What this does not establish

  • The book tables are unsafe timestamp proxies.

    The 2026-08-03 correction demoted every ts_bookdiff* output because the builder's tie-break, arrivals then fills then terminal statuses, is not HyperCore's documented action ordering. Every book-update number on this page inherits that.

  • A book update carrying a fill and a placement at the same microsecond cannot be split.

    The execution share in section 64.5 is therefore a lower bound on how mixed the book updates really are.

  • The book-event numbers cover 43% of each catalogue.

    Section 64.6 carries the surge-over-control comparison to every date at fill grain, a coarser measure whose level runs 12 to 17 points higher on the same events.

  • Every comparison is descriptive.

    Each is against a matched window or against the event's own past.

  • The unwind tilt is read on the 1-minute snapshot.

    A snapshot distance moves on its own when takers consume the levels in front of a standing quote. The placement-time measure, the distance to the touch at each order's own timestamp, is built in drafts/place0922_section.md. On the same rows, both measures size-weighted, it reads the unwind tilt at +0.35 bps against +0.49 on the snapshot and the accumulation tilt at +0.9 bps against -19.8, which is why section 64.3 folds the accumulation reading. Tables 4 and 5 are still to be recomputed at placement time.

  • The unwind tilt is a 2-hour window average on the older market-maker phase rule.

    The placement-time build splits the unwind into minute buckets from t*: its tilt peaks at +0.82 bps 5 to 10 minutes past the peak and is +0.10 bps by 120 to 360 minutes (drafts/place0922_section.md, Table 4 there). The split by the share of the peak excursion still held, 100-75, 75-50, 50-25 and 25-0%, and the current 4.4 rule of Table 3 remain to be built for this catalogue.

  • The class ordering in section 64.5 rests on 35 cascade units.

    Their interquartile range overlaps those of the other two classes.

69. What a print consumes and what comes back before the next trade

A taker print takes the surge-side quote away from the mid, and about a quarter of that distance is back before the next trade.

  • 24.6% of the distance consumed is replaced on a one-sided surge and 23.8% in a matched quiet window.
  • The share replaced rises with the size of the print, from 0.07 on the smallest tenth of prints inside an episode to 0.40 on the largest tenth.
  • The quote still ends further out after a large print: a net 2.68 bps at the top decile, against 0.09 bps back inside at the bottom decile.
  • The best level standing at the next trade holds 0.894 of the size that stood before the print, against 0.997 at the bottom decile.
Setup: the three quote readings, the population, and the fill timestamp parts

One row is one fill timestamp inside the surge window, the book update at which a fill occurred, and the next row is the next fill timestamp of any wallet. On the side the surge hits, with m the ts_bookdiff_lt mid at that timestamp and s = +1 when the surge side is the ask and -1 when it is the bid, so that away from the mid is positive:

name what it is where it is read
a0_pre the best quote on the surge side just before the taker print at t_i ts_bookdiff_lt at t_i
a0_post the best quote just after that print ts_bookdiff_le at t_i
a1_pre the best quote just before the next trade ts_bookdiff_lt at t_{i+1}, the next fill timestamp of any wallet
q(a0_pre), q(a1_pre) the resting size at the best level in those two states, in HYPE bid_0_amount or ask_0_amount of the same rows

Population. The F1 one-sided surges of tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv and the matched quiet windows of tables/redef2_pop_control_windows.csv, every date. A fill timestamp enters the sample when a taker execution consumed the surge side at t_i, which is tk_hype > 0 in the build's part files. Fill timestamps are kept only inside the fill timestamp build's surge window, [t0, t1 - 1 min) on a surge and [t0, t1) on a control.

Grain. Fill grain only. At book-event grain a1_pre equals a0_post by construction, because the row after le(t_i) is the same book state: measured here, the gap is non-zero on 0.119% of book updates at book-event grain. The gap carries information only when consecutive rows are further apart than one book update, which at fill grain means the next fill timestamp of any wallet.

Scope. data/tick0922_parts, the fill-grain fill timestamp build of section 64.6. 1,071,010 surge-side taker fill timestamps on 910 surges over 351 dates, 2025-03-30 to 2026-06-29, and 808,261 fill timestamps on 558 controls over 276 dates, 2025-03-31 to 2026-06-30. The surge catalogue holds three windows starting on 2025-10-10, contributing 19,522 fill timestamps, and three on 2026-01-31, contributing 3,167. The control catalogue holds no window starting on 2025-10-10 and five on 2026-01-31, contributing 7,598 fill timestamps. The 12 surges absent from the sample are one-minute runs, whose fill timestamp window [t0, t1 - 1 min) is empty.

Compute. code/tickq0922_decile_gaps.py, one pass over the fill-grain part files with an 8-worker pool on one soal node, under 2 minutes wall and about 3 GB peak memory. The figure is built by code/tickq0922_figure.py.

69.1 Definitions

Three distances in basis points, measured on the surge side at the fill timestamp t_i:

consumed      c = 1e4 * s * (a0_post - a0_pre) / m
replenished   r = 1e4 * s * (a1_pre  - a0_post) / m
net           d = c + r = 1e4 * s * (a1_pre - a0_pre) / m

Shares below are of surge fill timestamps.

  • c > 0: the print cleared the best level and pushed the quote away from the mid, 36.3%.
  • c = 0: the level absorbed the print with the price unchanged, 53.4%.
  • c < 0: a quote arrived inside the previous best at the same timestamp, 10.3%.
  • r < 0: the quote came back toward the mid before the next trade, 20.8%.
  • r > 0: the quote moved further out, 7.5%.
  • r = 0: the best quote stood unchanged between the two trades, 71.7%.

The replenishment ratio, defined on fill timestamps with c > 0, and the depth ratio, the best-level resting size at the next trade over the size before the print:

rho = -r / c                    1 = back at a0_pre before the next trade, 0 = no replacement
phi = q(a1_pre) / q(a0_pre)     1 = the same size is standing
  • Each fill timestamp is ranked into deciles of the surge-side taker dollars executed at that timestamp, tk_usd = tk_hype * m, within its own event, so prints are compared against other prints of the same episode. Decile 1 is the smallest tenth of prints inside the episode and decile 10 the largest.
  • The alternative ranking pools every fill timestamp of a population before cutting the deciles, dec_scheme = pooled in the same source file. It moves the surge medians by at most 0.24 bps on c and 0.012 on phi, both at decile 10, and rho by at most 0.024, at decile 7.

69.2 The decile ladder

Every measure moves with the size of the print, and the top decile is where the moves become large: from decile 1 to decile 10 the consumed distance runs 1.04 bps to 4.25 bps on the surges, the share replaced 0.07 to 0.40, and the depth standing at the next trade 0.997 to 0.894.

69.3 The regression form

A regression of the replacement on the push measures the decile ladder's relation in one number and carries a standard error. Conditional resiliency is the standard form.

  • The dependent variable is how much of the push comes back before the next trade. The regressor is the push itself.
  • An event fixed effect absorbs everything that makes one episode different from another, so the slope is identified from the variation in print size inside a single episode. The difference between a calm episode and a violent one is held by the fixed effect.
  • Standard errors are clustered by event, which lets the fill timestamps of one episode be arbitrarily correlated, as they are when one maker quotes the same way for the length of a surge.
r_i     = beta  * c_i + alpha_e(i) + u_i        beta  = share of the push replaced
log phi = gamma * c_i + alpha_e(i) + v_i        gamma = depth response, per bp

The regressor is c in every row. winsor is the treatment of both variables: none uses them as measured, 1/99 pct clips each at its own 1st and 99th percentile within the population, which matters because c reaches 913 bps on the surges and its standard deviation falls from 9.7 to 2.4 bps under the clip. r carries both treatments because they disagree on the surges; d and log phi are quoted on the clipped variables, and their raw rows are in the source file. Every row carries event fixed effects; the same specifications without them are in the source file under fixed_effects = none and move no slope in this table by more than 0.025. slope is the coefficient on c, cluster SE the standard error clustered by event, t the ratio of the two, within R2 the R-squared after the fixed effects. 69.4 Findings

As expected.

  • The quote replaces about a quarter of what a print takes, and the share rises with the print.

    Pooling every fill timestamp with c > 0, the replacement is 24.6% of the distance consumed on the surges and 23.8% in the matched windows. Ranked inside the episode, the mean ratio runs 0.07 at decile 1 to 0.40 at decile 10 on the surges and 0.06 to 0.36 on the controls (Tables 21 and 22).

  • A bigger print pushes the quote further and leaves it further out at the next trade.

    The consumed distance runs 1.04 bps at decile 1 to 4.25 bps at decile 10 on the surges, and the net distance at the next trade runs 0.09 bps back inside to 2.68 bps further out. The regression puts the same relation at 0.72 bps of net distance per bp consumed on the surges and 0.80 on the controls (Table 26).

  • The largest prints are the ones that clear the level.

    The share of fill timestamps where the print left the best price where it was falls from 0.77 at decile 1 to 0.14 at decile 10 on the surges, and from 0.82 to 0.26 on the controls, so most small prints are absorbed inside the standing best level.

  • The best level standing at the next trade is thinner after a bigger print.

    The depth ratio runs 0.997 at decile 1 to 0.894 at decile 10 on the surges. The mechanism is the level being eaten: on the fill timestamps where the price did not move the ratio falls to 0.597 at decile 10, while on the fill timestamps where it did move the level exposed behind the eaten one holds 1.11 times its size at decile 10 and 5.11 times at decile 1 (Table 23).

  • Bigger prints are followed sooner by the next trade.

    The median gap to the next fill runs 350 ms at decile 1 to 251 ms at decile 10 on the surges, against 714 ms to 461 ms on the controls, so the surge measurement window is about half the control's throughout, and the whole ladder is measured over a shorter interval on the surges.

  • Liquidation cascades push hardest per print at the top deciles.

    At deciles 8 to 10 the consumed distance is 2.69 bps in a cascade and 2.47 bps on a big price move, against 2.14 bps with no big price move, on 46, 312 and 552 events (Table 24).

Not as expected (possible design cause).

  • The raw and the clipped slope disagree on the surges.

    The raw slope is -0.036 with a clustered standard error of 0.028 against -0.187 with 0.017 clipped, while on the controls the two bracket each other at -0.264 and -0.191. Possible design cause: 1,465 surge fill timestamps on 140 events carry c above 50 bps, up to 913 bps on 2025-10-10 at 21:17:41, and those pushes are followed by almost no replacement before the next trade, which a level-on-level ordinary least squares reads as a flatter slope. The clipped row is the one to quote; both are kept.

  • The surge and the control replace the same share of a push.

    The slope is -0.187 against -0.191 on all sample fill timestamps and -0.228 against -0.264 on the fill timestamps with c > 0, so the quote comes back at the same rate per basis point pushed in both populations. Possible design cause: the two populations are measured over different windows, a median 290 ms to the next trade on a surge against 616 ms in a control, so the control has twice as long to replace the same push. Check: recompute both at a fixed clock horizon, which section 64.7 already does in event time and clock time for the push-reversion share.

  • The replacement share falls with the push on the surges and rises on the controls at the top of the range.

    Above 10 bps the aggregate replacement is 0.213 on the surges and 0.417 on the controls, against 0.379 and 0.251 at or below 1 bp (Table 25). Possible design cause: a push above 10 bps in a quiet window is usually one wide price step that a maker steps back into, while the same push inside a surge is a sweep through several levels that nobody refills before the next print arrives 250 ms later. Check: split the above-10-bps bucket by the taker's n_levels and by whether the surge-side quote already stood more than one fill timestamp from the mid.

  • Conditional on the print moving the quote, a bigger move goes with a slightly thinner replacement level.

    The slope is -0.008 in log depth per bp with a clustered standard error of 0.003 on the surges and -0.015 with 0.005 on the controls, against +0.110 and +0.271 on the full sample. Possible design cause: phi mixes two states, and the positive full-sample slope is the mix moving from the c = 0 state, where phi sits below 1, toward the c > 0 state, where it sits above 1. Inside the c > 0 state the remaining variation is which level was sitting behind the one eaten, and the relation is measurable but small: a 5 bp push goes with a level 4% thinner.

  • The depth ratio at c > 0 falls from decile 1 to decile 10 here, while section 64.5 reports it falling to a basin over deciles 4 to 8 and rising again to decile 10.

    Possible design cause: the two are different measurements. That section is at book-event grain on the big-price-move class, ranks on executed size including maker fills, and keeps only fill timestamps the print pushed; this table is at fill grain, ranks on taker dollars, and keeps every surge-side taker fill timestamp.

69.5 Validation

Every check in tables/tickq0922_validation.csv passes
  • Per decile the fill timestamp counts sum to the population total, 1,071,010 on the surges and 808,261 on the controls, under both ranking schemes, and the ten decile rows of each table sum to its all-decile row.
  • Deciles are balanced inside an event: across the 902 surges with at least 50 sample fill timestamps, the median share of an event's fill timestamps falling in a decile runs 0.0996 to 0.1004 over the ten deciles, and the same range holds across the 558 controls.
  • d equals c + r on all 1,879,271 fill timestamps to 0, and the shares of fill timestamps with c > 0, c = 0 and c < 0 sum to 1 on every fill timestamp.
  • Rerunning the tick0922_by_decile recipe on these parts, with its own filters and its own ranking on executed size, reproduces all 480 of its grain = fill rows with a largest absolute difference of 9.1e-13. The sample here is larger, 1,071,010 against 392,705 surge fill timestamps, because this build keeps every surge-side taker fill timestamp including the ones where the price did not move.
  • Every date the catalogues reach is present, 351 dates on the surges and 276 on the controls, including 2025-10-10 with 19,522 surge fill timestamps from three windows and 2026-01-31 with 3,167 from three. The control catalogue holds no window starting on 2025-10-10 and five on 2026-01-31, which contribute 7,598 fill timestamps.
  • At book-event grain the gap a1_pre - a0_post is non-zero on 0.119% of the 439,869 surge-side taker fill timestamps, confirming that it is zero by construction at that grain.
  • Dropping the 2025-03-24 to 2025-05-25 dates, where the maker and taker fill rows do not balance, moves the surge ratio from 0.301 to 0.298 on 801 events and the control ratio from 0.211 to 0.214 on 491. Those dates hold 7.0% of the surge fill timestamps and 6.2% of the control fill timestamps.
  • Fill timestamps where only a maker fill row exists on the surge side, 1.1% on the surges and 1.8% on the controls, sit outside the sample, which requires a taker execution.

69.6 What this does not establish

  • "The next trade" is the next fill timestamp of any wallet.

    It can be a print on either side of the book. The replacement window is a median 290 ms on a surge and 616 ms in a control, so the two populations are compared over windows of different length, and the surge-minus-control comparisons in Table 26 carry that difference inside them.

  • The gap is identically zero at book-event grain.

    Nothing here reads as a statement about what happens between two consecutive book updates. It is a statement about what happens between two trades.

  • r mixes new quotes with cancels.

    A value of r < 0 means the best quote ended nearer the mid than a0_post, which a placement inside and a cancel further out both produce; nothing here attributes the replacement to any wallet or to the market makers specifically. Attribution needs the order store, which the fill timestamp build does not read.

  • The deciles are a ranking, not a treatment.

    A fill timestamp lands in decile 10 because the taker chose to send a large order at that moment, which is also when the book was thin or the price was moving, so the ladder describes what follows a large print, and the causal reading stays open.

  • The event fixed effect absorbs the episode, not the minute.

    Within one surge the early and late minutes differ in depth and in spread, and the slope pools them.

70. What separates the surges whose price reverts from those that hold

Whether the price of a one-sided taker surge is still standing 15 minutes later is decided by the taker flow that arrives after the run ends.

  • The median event that holds takes another $0.43m of net taker volume in the surge direction over those 15 minutes. The median event that reverts meets $3.16m of net taker volume against it.
  • The surge-side quote says the same over the same 15 minutes, traveling 0.97, 1.04 and 1.10 bps back toward the mid for every 1 bps away across the events that hold, the partly reverted and the reverted.
  • Everything measured while the run is under way reads the same across the three patterns: the market-maker population's unwind tilt, the execution and cancel shares of the quote's travel, the surge-side depth and the size of the surge itself.
Setup: population, grain, windows, sources

One row is one event. The population is the 922 F1 one-sided taker surges of tables/redef4_price_class.csv (family == 'F1'), carrying the price pattern of record (project record, section 41.4): 206 held, 224 partly reverted, 62 reverted (492 gated events), 428 with a small price move, whose peak move stays below the gate g, and 2 against. The small-price-move events are a reference column throughout; the 2 against events are counted in validation and not tabulated.

Every date in the sample is included, 2025-10-10 and 2026-01-31 among them, 351 dates with three events on each of those two. The gated runs last 15 minutes at the median (p5 5, p25 11, p75 25, p95 42).

Sources, all experiment-local: the price pattern, anchors and peak move from tables/redef4_price_class.csv and tables/redef4_events_F1_one_sided.csv; taker flow in 1-minute bins from data/market_taker_1m.parquet; the market-maker population from tables/redef2_pop_event_mm_F1.csv, rows with shocked_loose == True, the accumulating population of section 64.3; quote travel at the book from surge-side fill timestamps rebuilt by code/rev0922_reverted_vs_held.py --stage ticks into data/rev0922_tick_parts/, from the same inputs as the fill-grain build; spread and depth by phase from tables/f1r0921_spread_phase_event.csv.

The surge side is the side the takers consumed, the ask for a buy surge and the bid for a sell surge.

Builder code/rev0922_reverted_vs_held.py, run 2026-09-22. Tables tables/rev0922_by_pattern.csv, _spearman.csv, _ols.csv, _excursion_baselines.csv, _cascade_top10.csv, _validation.csv and the per-event feature table _event_features.csv.

70.1 Definitions

The outcome.

  • rho_15 = M_final(15) / M_peak is the share of the peak move still standing at t1 + 15 min. Both moves run in the surge direction and are anchored on p_start, the first mid at t0.
  • M_peak is the furthest mid over [t0, t1 + 15 min).
  • The pattern of record splits the gated events at rho_15 >= 0.75 (held), 0.25 <= rho_15 < 0.75 (partly reverted) and rho_15 < 0.25 (reverted).
  • An event is gated when its peak move clears g, the full-sample p95 of the 1-minute peak move for its length class. An event whose peak move stays below g is a small price move.

The run window and the window after it. The run is [t0, t1), whose length in minutes reproduces the catalogue's own length_min_1m on all 922 events. The window after the run is [t1, t1 + 15 min), which ends where rho_15 reads its mid.

Taker flow. With d = +1 on a buy surge and d = -1 on a sell surge, the surge-side USD is the taker volume on side d inside the run and the opposite-side USD is the taker volume on side -d. The flow after the run is

net_post = d * (taker buy USD - taker sell USD)   over [t1, t1 + 15 min)

so positive means the flow keeps pushing the price the way the surge pushed it. The forced share is liquidation taker USD over all taker USD inside the run.

Market-maker tilt. Window family ②.

  • tilt_bps = d(SAME) - d(OPP) against the same market maker's own PRE2H value, in that market maker's own ACC and UNW windows as Table 3 defines them. Positive when the exit quote sits nearer the touch.
  • The event's value is the median across its accumulating market makers.
  • The two side distances are reported separately, each as d(side, phase) - d(side, PRE2H), positive when that side's best quote moved away from the mid.
  • The exit-side size share is size(OPP) / (size(OPP) + size(SAME)).
  • The accumulation readings are folded in section 70.3, for the reason section 64.3 gives.

Quote travel at the book. On the surge side, at every timestamp t_i at which a fill occurred, with m_i the pre-event mid and s = +1 on the ask, -1 on the bid,

c_bps      = 1e4 * s * (le(t_i)     - lt(t_i))  / m_i   what the fills and cancels did
r_bps      = 1e4 * s * (lt(t_{i+1}) - le(t_i))  / m_i   what happened before the next fill
away_total = sum(c_bps > 0) + sum(r_bps > 0)            gross travel away from the mid
  • away_total splits into trade, mixed, cancel at a fill and between fills by the fill-grain rule of section 64.6. The execution share is the trade part over away_total.
  • The mirror quantity is the gross travel back toward the mid, the negative parts of the same two terms. Their ratio is above 1 when the quote ends the window nearer the mid than it started.
  • The share of an executed push undone at 5 s and 30 s is 1 - (quote at the horizon - quote before the push) / c_bps, median over the run's executed pushes. A negative value means the quote kept traveling away.

Spread and depth. Window family ①.

  • PEAK_c is the 3 minutes [t_c - 1 min, t_c + 2 min), PRE2H the 2 hours before t0.
  • The spread ratio is the mean spread in PEAK_c over the mean spread in PRE2H, both computed as in section 64.4.
  • The depth ratio is the median resting size within 10 bps of the mid over the same two windows.

Sign convention and the two tests.

  • Every signed separator is named for the direction it measures and carries the sign its mechanism predicts for the Spearman against rho_15 (expected_sign_vs_rho15 in tables/rev0922_spearman.csv). The oriented Spearman, rho_oriented = rho * expected_sign, is positive when the mechanism holds. Measures with no directional prediction carry sign 0 and no oriented value.
  • The Kruskal-Wallis H test asks whether the three gated patterns draw their values of a separator from the same distribution, using ranks only.
  • The Spearman rho is the correlation of the ranks of a separator with the ranks of rho_15 across the 492 gated events.
  • With 32 separators tested, the Bonferroni threshold is 0.05 / 32 = 0.0016.

Figure 8. Eight candidate separators by price pattern.

What one mark is, and what the figure excludes

One panel per separator, dot at the median and bar from p25 to p75 over the events of that pattern; each panel carries its own event count because the market-maker and book measures are missing on some events. The small-price-move events are the reference column and are excluded from every rank test. Panel 1 is the surge's size, panels 2 and 3 the flow and the quote over the 15 minutes after the run, panel 4 the population's unwind tilt, panels 5 and 6 the book decomposition inside the run, and panels 7 and 8 the spread and depth around the pressure peak, each against the event's own prior 2 hours. The horizontal rule is 0 where a measure is signed and 1 where it is a ratio. The accumulation tilt is left out for the reason section 64.3 gives; its values are in Table 29.

70.2 Taker flow

The size of the surge separates the gated events from the small price moves and reads the same across the gated patterns.

  • The events that revert are the ones the flow turns against afterwards, meeting 0.23 of the run's own volume in the opposite direction over the next 15 minutes, against 0.03 more in the surge direction on the events that hold.

Column key and source

One row is one separator; cells are p5 to p95 across the events of that pattern, one value per line. An event's value is the median across the market makers that accumulated inventory during it, the shocked_loose population of the F1 population build, 6,173 rows of 118,269 spread over 849 of the 922 events. n gated is the number of the 492 gated events carrying that separator; the rest have no accumulating market maker (14 events) or no resting order on the side and window the measure needs. Tilt is d(SAME) - d(OPP) against the same market maker's own PRE2H value, positive when the exit quote sits nearer the touch. A side distance is positive when that side's best quote moved away from the mid. A side's distance is the market maker's nearest resting order on that side, in bps from the minute's mid, read on a 1-minute grid. The last two rows are counts and sums over the accumulating market makers, not medians. 70.4 Quote travel at the book

Executions move about three quarters of the surge-side quote's travel away from the mid in every pattern: 0.756 on the events that hold, 0.778 on the partly reverted and 0.784 on the events that revert. Cancels move 4% in all three.

  • The book measure that orders with the outcome sits after the run and is the price path read off the quote. Over the 15 minutes after the run the surge-side quote travels 0.968 bps back toward the mid for every 1 bps away on the events that hold, 1.041 on the partly reverted and 1.101 on the events that revert, on 492 events with no missing value.

70.8 The peak excursion on a longer baseline

A longer baseline makes every peak move larger and every event look more held.

M_peak is anchored on p_start, the first mid at t0.

  • Re-anchored on the median mid over the 2, 6 and 12 hours before t0, the median gated peak move goes from 260 bps on the t0 mid to 335, 382 and 410 bps, and the median gated rho_15 from 0.68 to 0.74.
  • Held to the same bands with the gate unchanged, 384 of the 492 gated events keep their pattern on the 2-hour baseline. Of the 108 that move, 47 partly reverted events become held and 36 reverted events become partly reverted.
  • Some gated events peak below their own baseline: 6 on the 2-hour median mid, 18 on the 6-hour and 33 on the 12-hour.

One row is one measure; cells are p5 to p95 across the events of that pattern, one value per line, all 922 events covered. A baseline is the median of the 1-minute mid over the window before t0, and M_peak on it is 1e4 * d * (p_peak / baseline - 1) in bps and d * (p_peak - baseline) in dollars, with d the surge direction.
